title: Hand and foot
hook: as hands and feet are parts of one body, beings are parts of one life (Bodhicaryavatara 8.91)
tomorrow: what if you traded places for an hour?

segments.voice: Yesterday: equalizing self and other. Everyone wants happiness, not pain, just as I do. But wanting the same thing isn't quite being one.
screen: `JUST AS I DO.` → `SAME WISH. ONE BODY?`

segments.voice: Stub your toe in the dark and watch what happens. Before a single thought, your hand is down there, holding the foot. Nobody asked the hand. It didn't stop to think, that's the foot's problem. It didn't check whether the toe deserved help. So is a stranger's pain my business the way my foot's pain is? Shantideva says yes, and then he lets an objector argue back.
screen: `A STUBBED TOE IN THE DARK.` → `THE HAND DOESN'T ASK.` → `AN OBJECTOR ARGUES BACK.`

segments.voice: His picture: the body has many parts, hands and feet and all the rest, yet we protect it as one. In the same way, beings are many, yet one in wanting happiness and fearing pain. Then the objection, voiced inside the poem, and it's a strong one: their pain doesn't hurt me. My foot's pain I feel; a stranger's, I don't. Why guard against what I can't feel? Give that side its due. It's honest, and it sounds like common sense. Shantideva's reply: then why protect your future self? Next year's pain doesn't hurt you now, yet you save for it and lock the door against it. You already care for someone you can't feel. 'Mine' was never about feeling; it's a habit of where we draw the line. Christian neighbors know a cousin of this picture. Paul, in the King James English: "the eye cannot say unto the hand, I have no need of thee." One honest difference: Paul's body is the church, joined in Christ; Shantideva's takes in every being who can feel. One body.
screen: `MANY PARTS, ONE BODY.` · `THE OBJECTION: I DON'T FEEL IT.` · `YOU GUARD YOUR FUTURE SELF.` · `I HAVE NO NEED OF THEE.` · then, large: `ONE BODY.`

segments.voice: Let one hand rest gently on the other wrist, or on your knee, or on your foot if you can reach it. Feel how the hand looks after it without asking whose it is. Then bring to mind one person whose trouble you could ease a little, the way this hand would.
Hand and foot: Shantideva's picture of beings as parts of one life, cared for the way a hand cares for a foot.
The line for today: one body; the hand doesn't ask whose foot it is. Day thirty-nine of the guide.

howItsDone: Tibetan Buddhist teachers use Shantideva's hand-and-foot image when teaching compassion practice, inviting students to widen the circle of what they count as 'mine' to care for.

match.prompt: one body, two voices — tap the pairs.

fork.setup: your friend says, 'one body sounds nice, but i can't feel your headache.' what's the strongest form of her point?
options: pain is felt one person at a time, so 'mine' seems to draw a natural line.
anyone who says 'one body' secretly doesn't care about real people.
the idea only works for people you already love.
fork.reveal: that's the objector's case in the poem, and it's honest. Shantideva's reply: you already care for your future self, whose pain you can't feel yet.

trapdoor: what you thought: we're all one, a poster slogan.
what it means: beings are many but share the wish for happiness, so care can cross the line of 'mine'.
what a scholar hears: the image comes as the guide moves from equalizing toward exchange; the objection and the future-self reply follow a few verses on.
guess: caring for others the way one hand cares for a foot
dividing the chores evenly between two people
working hard with your whole body, head to toe

chat.says: ava sprained her wrist. her mural's due friday. mine's due monday. mom says do yours first. is she wrong?
options: her point's fair. but a hand helps a foot: give ava a few hours, then do yours.
mom's right. ava's wrist isn't your pain; you can't feel it, so it isn't your job.
drop your piece completely. if you're one body, your deadline doesn't count.
chat.meaning: Shantideva says beings are like parts of one body: help as a hand helps a foot, without pretending your own part doesn't matter.

Shantideva.meaning: the Indian monk-poet who wrote the guide to the bodhisattva's way

Paul.meaning: an early Christian apostle who wrote letters to churches

King James.meaning: a classic English translation of the Bible
